title: Reinforcing High-Entropy Alloy Composites and Exploring the Impacts of Various Reinforcement Fillers on Microstructure and Mechanical Characterizations: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Abstract A recently-developed category of structural materials, known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has attracted great attention among researchers due to their considerable mechanical, thermal, and even chemical durability. When it comes to strength-enhancing reinforcements in composites, the type of used reinforcing agents is crucial in controlling mechanical behavior and achieving the desired microstructure. In fact, designing diverse types of reinforcements such as carbides, oxides, intermetallics, and carbon-based nanomaterials has a significant impact on enhancing the ultimate performance of HEAs. Meanwhile, among different synthesis approaches, powder metallurgy (PM) has proved to be among the best methods for controlling the microstructure and composition, resulting in the formation of homogeneous particle dispersion in a refined microstructure. Hybrid reinforcements are engineered to enhance mechanical properties by engaging multiple strengthening mechanisms, such as Orowan strengthening and grain refining, leading to high ultimate compressive strength (UCS) and compressive yield strength (CYS) along with enhanced ductility and fracture resistance. To achieve synergistic reinforcing effects, future studies should focus on developing gradient and hybrid reinforcement systems that efficiently integrate carbonaceous nanostructures, oxides, and ceramics. Additionally, employing a mixture of various reinforcements such as carbides and oxides may yield complementary effects. Advancements in computer modeling and machine learning are recommended for optimizing processing conditions and reinforcement design, while in-situ characterization during high-temperature experiments is essential to understand the unique strengthening behaviors of different reinforcement types on the hardness of HEA composites. This review meticulously evaluated the important role of reinforcing types and their subsequent impacts on designing next-generation HEAs with customized microstructure, activating efficient strengthening mechanisms, and even enhancing the mechanical properties for various crucial applications such as aerospace, nuclear, and tooling.
journal: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Major breakthroughs in research on modern materials have been strengthened by the invention of a novel class of materials, known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), that has significantly changed alloy design approaches [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. Development of HEAs has been increasing rapidly since Cantor et al. [ 6 ] and Yeh et al. [ 7 ] proposed them almost simultaneously in 2004. Due to their compositionally complex nature, HEAs have a variety of remarkable properties as well as distinctive microstructural features [ 8 ], which let them perform better than traditional alloy systems [ 5 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 ]. The idea of designing a multi-elemental alloy generates high configurational entropy of mixing [ 12 ], which ultimately leads to the formation of a stable solid-solution phase [ 13 ,  14 ]. Despite impressive performance, HEAs have not yet entirely met their potential, especially among applications which require high mechanical durability [ 15 ,  16 – 17 ]. The principle of composite materials continues to thrive throughout decades of effective operation [ 18 ,  19 ] and their previous performance signifies their capability to inspire innovation. From this perspective, an achievable strategy for further enhancement of the mechanical properties of HEAs is through the thoughtful incorporation of reinforcements in composite design concepts [ 16 ,  17 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 – 25 ]. In addition, HEAs can be considered as promising candidates for emerging composite materials owing to their superior mechanical properties and effective nanoparticle reinforcement [ 26 ]. Regarding fabrication techniques, various strategies have been developed to produce particle-reinforced HEA composites (HEACs) [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]. Due to the fact that reinforcement dispersion and interfacial properties are extremely vulnerable to processing conditions, processing step has a more significant effect on the properties of HEACs compared to its influence on all HEAs [ 33 ]. Even though casting-based fabrication techniques, particularly vacuum arc melting, have been widely employed for the fabrication of HEAs due to their ability to melt and solidify several elements with various melting points, they are neither appropriate nor directly useful for the fabrication of particle-reinforced HEACs. In fact, elemental segregation is considerably notable during liquid-state fabrications which can be due to big differences in melting temperature and thermal conductivity among metallic matrices and reinforcing particles as well as the challenges of maintaining even distribution of reinforcement. This issue has resulted in the various challenges such as reinforcement agglomeration, microstructural inconsistency and shrinkage porosity [ 34 ,  35 – 36 ]. Indeed, reinforcements are typically more prone to agglomeration when produced using melting-based processing techniques, making them less appealing for manufacturing of such materials using these techniques [ 37 ,  38 ]. As an alternative, a solid-state method called powder metallurgy (PM), offers better control over microstructural changes and improves reinforcement distribution [ 36 ,  39 ]. Consequently, PM has gained growing attention as an effective fabrication strategy for compositionally complex HEAs, confirming its applicability for the fabrication of HEACs with dense, uniform and refined microstructures [ 35 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ]. PM is typically defined as the fabrication of powders and their following consolidation into a cohesive and dense solid form [ 40 ]. Each of these steps relies on well-defined methods which can ensure the achievement of desired material properties; therefore, a profound investigation and comparison of these methods is crucial for optimizing the performance of the final product.

Beyond processing considerations, another contributing factor governing the performance of HEACs is the nature of the reinforcing phase itself [ 43 ,  44 ]. Although a wide variety of reinforcing phases have been employed to enhance the mechanical properties of HEACs, most reported data are often confined to individual systems and remain highly scattered and system-specific [ 23 ,  24 ,  45 ,  46 ]. Consequently, a comparative analysis for understanding and assessing how different reinforcement types influence mechanical performance is still lacking. The present review serves to fill this gap by conducting a comparative investigation on different reinforcement types incorporated into HEACs fabricated by PM-based methods, with emphasis on their mechanical strengthening effects. Figure  1  depicts the complex structure of HEAs. It emphasizes the important and decisive role of reinforcement type and compositional design strategy in determining favorable mechanical performance through activating multiple strengthening mechanisms, which is discussed comprehensively throughout this study. The goal is to provide a suitable framework for designing next-generation HEACs with customized properties.

sections.heading: PM and its Processing Routes in Reinforced HEAs
paragraphs: PM represents a manufacturing procedure in which mixed powdered materials are compressed and subsequently sintered to form solid components [ 47 ]. This approach enables even dispersion of reinforcing agents and considerable control over the final properties and facilitates the fabrication of complicated geometries with unique material compositions [ 41 ,  48 ,  49 ]. Moreover, due to the fact that they can facilitate the integration of ceramic, intermetallic and nano-scale reinforcements into HEA systems [ 50 ,  51 ,  52 – 53 ], PM-based methods can be considered as highly effective routes for the development of HEACs. Having established PM as the most preferred, versatile and effective route for producing reinforced HEACs, it is essential to examine the specific processing strategies that fall under this category. Therefore, particular attention is given to powder preparation and consolidation, the two principal processes of PM route, which play decisive roles in achieving microstructural uniformity, well-dispersed reinforcements, and enhanced mechanical and tribological performance in HEACs [ 41 ,  54 ].

sections.heading: Powder Preparation
paragraphs: Powder preparation, as the initial stage of PM, mainly involves the selection, mixing and blending of appropriate powder materials [ 54 ]. This stage is of critical importance, as the quality of the subsequent PM processes heavily depends on it [ 48 ,  55 ]. Regarding the composites, the significance of powder mixing becomes even more critical because having a homogenous mixture with an even distribution of reinforcement particles is essential for successful fabrication of HEACs [ 49 ]. Mechanical alloying (MA) and atomization are the two main approaches at this stage [ 40 ]. Among them, MA is regarded as the most effective and widely adopted technique [ 56 ]. A better dispersion of reinforcements as well as high compositional accuracy could be achieved in HEACs through MA [ 57 ,  58 ]. To be more specific, owing to their high level of adaptability, when it comes to more complicated HEA structures, MA outperforms conventional melting and casting approaches [ 59 ]. In this process, elemental powders undergo repeated cold welding, deformation, fracturing, and rewelding inside a high-energy ball mill, which provide solid-state diffusion and atomic-level alloying. Therefore, this high-energy process produces ultrafine, compositionally uniform powders while minimizing elemental segregation and ensuring homogeneous reinforcement dispersion [ 54 ,  60 ,  61 ]. Popescu et al. [ 59 ] successfully fabricated AlCrFeNiMn HEAs and graphite-reinforced HEACs through MA, followed by compaction and sintering. Conversely, gas and water atomization produce fine, spherical, pre-alloyed powders via rapid solidification. Gas atomization provides high-purity powders with excellent flowability and narrow particle size distribution; whereas water atomization offers a cost-effective alternative but typically introduces slightly higher oxygen content [ 62 ].

sections.heading: Powder Consolidation
paragraphs: In PM, compacted powders can be transformed into dense, cohesive and high-strength solids through consolidation and sintering processes. Heating during these processes allows bonding among particles, thereby decreasing porosity and developing customized microstructures and properties [ 63 ]. Utilizing approaches such as cold compaction, hot pressing, or hot isostatic pressing, elemental or pre-alloyed powders get compressed into the desired shape during consolidation. The compact is subsequently subjected to high temperatures below its melting point during the sintering process, which facilitates diffusion and metallurgical bonding. These approaches improve strength, grain cohesion, and dimensional stability. In complicated techniques such as spark plasma sintering (SPS), concurrently applied pressure and pulsed current promote densification, consequently generating almost fully dense components with finer grains and superior mechanical performance. By precisely controlling the parameters of sintering including temperature, pressure, and dwell duration, PM enables the improvement of microstructural features and functional performance in HEAs and advanced HEACs [ 10 ]. Figure  2  depicts PM process, which begins with powder preparation, followed by MA, atomization, consolidation, and sintering to produce a dense bulk matrix or composite.

Fig. 2 Schematic illustration of the PM process route, representing powder preparation through MA and atomization, followed by consolidation and sintering resulting in either a dense bulk matrix or a dense reinforced bulk composite

sections.heading: Classification of Reinforcement Fillers
paragraphs: As discussed in the introduction section, the adoption of composite strategy particularly in the context of HEACs through the incorporation of different reinforcement fillers has demonstrated considerable potential for enhancing the mechanical properties and functional performance of HEAs. Accordingly, in this section, we will go through various categories of reinforcements in detail and critically review the successful and promising outcomes in existing literature. Reinforcement fillers used in HEACs can be broadly classified into oxides, carbides, borides, nitrides, carbon-based reinforcements, hybrid and other metallic reinforcements, as summarized in Fig.  3 .

Fig. 3 Classification of reinforcement types that can be added to HEAs, including carbide-based, carbon-based, oxide-based (including various oxides of transition metals, rare-earth oxide (REO)-based, alumina (Al 2 O 3 ), etc.), hybrid reinforcements (mixture of several types) and, other reinforcements (such as nitride or boride, as well as those not mentioned in previous categories)

sections.heading: Carbon-Based Fillers
paragraphs: Carbon-based reinforcements, particularly carbon nanostructures, have attracted considerable attention for strengthening HEAs due to their exceptional mechanical properties and nanoscale reinforcement effects. For instance, adding carbon nanotubes (CNTs) as reinforcements into TiZrVMnCu-Er HEACs significantly enhanced hardness and compressive strength. These enhancements were attributed to grain refinement strengthening, load transfer influences, and fracture bridging/deflection mechanisms triggered by CNTs [ 64 ]. Likewise, AlCoFeMnNi/CNTs nanocomposites showed considerable improvement in shear strength when compared with non-reinforced HEAs. A long-term MA in this system led to a complete formation of solid-solution phases. Moreover, using effective load transfer, the stabilization of grain boundaries and the uniform dispersion of CNTs, microstructural refinement and strengthening could be achieved [ 65 ]. Furthermore, it has been found that the addition of graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) into CoCrFeNiMn HEAs can considerably enhance their mechanical performance. The strengthened composites exhibited higher tensile and compressive strength while maintaining excellent ductility, mainly as a result of grain refinement, effective stress transfer, and controlled crack propagation and twin formation mechanisms [ 66 ]. To further explore the reinforcing potential of graphene, another investigation reported that graphene-encapsulated CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles were utilized as building blocks for fabricating bulk composites, resulting in substantial improvements in hardness, yield strength, and wear resistance [ 25 ]. In another study, Doan et al. [ 67 ] investigated the mechanical behavior of AlCrFeCuNi/graphene nanocomposites. In this simulation study, graphene was shown to enhance strength and stiffness by promoting effective load transfer and restricting dislocation motion at the interface. More recently, to take advantage of their complementary strengthening effects, hybrid reinforcements that combine CNTs and GNPs have been developed to take advantage of their complementary strengthening mechanisms. In particular, a structure based on CNTs and GNPs reinforcements in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs achieved a superior balance of strength and ductility, confirming that synergistic reinforcement outperformed the use of either CNTs or GNPs alone [ 68 ]. Similarly, in another investigation on CrCoFeMnNi HEAs produced by MA and SPS [ 69 ], hybrid carbonaceous reinforcements CNTs and GNPs not only improved hardness and tensile strength but also increased wear resistance by promoting the formation of self-lubricating surfaces. It is worth mentioning that the effectiveness of CNTs-GNPs as a hybrid carbon-based reinforcement system has been demonstrated in various composite systems, where it consistently outperformed individual carbon-based fillers. In fact, comparable trends have also been reported in other studies, indicating that the beneficial effects of this combination were not coincidental and CNTs-GNPs hybrid reinforcing system could be considered as a promising candidate in composites [ 70 ]. These investigations have indicated the great potential of hybrid approaches in reaching a balance between strength and ductility, along with the versatility of carbon-based reinforcements in HEAs.

sections.heading: Carbide Fillers
paragraphs: High-entropy ceramics (HECEs) are an innovative class of materials which contain unique compositions and can enhance the ultimate properties of the products compared to traditional ceramics, including their hot hardness, thermal stability at elevated temperatures, and resistance to corrosion. These unique combinations make them well-suited for applications in harsh environments, such as extreme temperatures, corrosive conditions, and high-stress situations. The performance of these ceramics is strongly affected by the elements present in their matrix, as well as key parameters such as their atomic size and valence electron concentration [ 71 ]. Many researchers have been working on HECEs [ 71 ,  72 – 73 ]. For example, Verma et al. [ 71 ] discussed the importance of atomic size compatibility among constituent metallic powders in order to achieve homogeneous mixing and entropic stabilization in HECs. Figure  4 , which is reported by Verma et al. [ 71 ], shows various types of HECEs, broadly classified into carbide, boride, nitride, silicide, oxide, ceramics and the like according to the main constituent element. In fact, this figure can assist in visualizing diversity in HECs through depicting how the selection of principal element can affect ceramic classification and impact its specific properties and potential applications.
Fig. 4 Various categories of HECEs based on their primary constituent elements [ 71 ]

Among different types of HECEs, high-entropy carbides are distinctive due to their exceptional hardness and outstanding thermal, electrical, mechanical, and oxidation resistance properties. When it comes to carbide-based reinforcements, they have shown significant efficiency as reinforcements in HEAs. As an example, enhancing microhardness, fracture toughness, and wear resistance is reported for CuFeNiMnTi HEAs due to the in-situ formation of titanium carbides [ 74 ]. Another reported study related to the fabrication of FeMnNiCrAlSiC HEAs via MA showed the increasing of hardness and wear resistance, which was due to the formation of carbide. This study emphasized the ability of carbide-containing HEAs for applications demanding enhanced wear resistance [ 75 ]. In order to demonstrate the benefits of carbides, titanium carbide (TiC) nanoparticles have been added into CoCrFeMnNi HEAs by means of water atomization, MA, and SPS. The addition of TiC led to grain refinement and obvious enhancements in compressive yield and fracture strength, without sacrificing ductility [ 76 ]. Confirming these findings, PM-fabricated W x TaTiVCr HEAs showed considerable enhancement of hardness and strength caused by the formation of solid-solution and dispersion strengthening from the homogenous formation of in-situ TiC in the matrix. In fact, the formation of these fine precipitations during sintering process was shown to improve microstructure and efficiently hinder the movement of dislocations, thereby confirming the significant role of carbide dispersion in the strengthening of refractory HEAs [ 77 ]. Moreover, research has shown that during the annealing of carbon-doped FeCoCrNiMn HEAs, the formation of fine M₂₃C₆ carbides could significantly enhance mechanical performance. In fact, the presence of these nano-sized carbides efficiently suppressed grain growth during recrystallization and also served as major obstacles to dislocation movements. Accordingly, the alloy benefited from simultaneous effects of precipitation strengthening as well as grain refinement, which resulted in a considerable enhancement of strength while retaining sufficient ductility [ 78 ]. Additionally, FeCoNiCrMn HEAs boosted in-situ hydrocarbon additives, ex-situ TiC, and tantalum carbide (TaC) had better hardness and wear resistance. This enhancement was mainly achieved through the simultaneous effects of grain refinement and carbide strengthening. The fine formed carbides during processing could result in the restriction of both grain growth and dislocation movements, while plastic deformation during sliding was prevented by the presence of hard TiC and TaC particles [ 79 ]. In addition to TiC, another important carbide which has been widely studied as reinforcement in HEAs is silicon carbide (SiC); for instance, PM-fabricated CoCrNiMnFe HEAs reinforced with SiC particles obtained excellent compression strength and hardness [ 80 ]. Similarly, the addition of evenly distributed SiC particles into FeCoNiCrAl HEAs could result in grain refinement as well as dramatic hardness enhancement [ 81 ]. Aside from SiC particle reinforcement, it has been reported that the employment of SiC whiskers (SiC w ) enhanced the toughness and wear resistance of high-entropy nitride ceramics (HENCs). Indeed, the development of a compact microstructure was reported through the addition of SiC w  in SPS-fabricated (HfNbTaTiZr)N composites [ 82 ]. In contrast to traditional SiC particles, SiC w  showed a high aspect ratio which stimulated active interaction of cracks. The presence of whiskers along grain boundaries could deflect and bridge cracks, absorbing fracture energy and restricting crack growth. This mechanism resulted in the enhancement of toughness, structural stability, and wears resistance. Thus, SiC reinforced the mechanical and tribological performance of HEACs regardless of their morphology. Similarly, in-situ precipitation of Cr₇C₃ carbides at graphene oxide interfaces in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs could lead to the improvement of microhardness and reduction of wear rate due to their strong interfacial bonding [ 83 ]. Moreover, in PM-fabricated tungsten carbide (WC)-reinforced CrFeCoNi HEAs, it was reported that the presence of a uniform dispersion of hard WC particles as well as the simultaneous formation of chromium carbides within the matrix resulted in the enhancement of mechanical and tribological properties. In fact, these carbide particles could not only act as load-carrying constituents but also result in microstructural refinement and impediment of dislocation movements. Moreover, the enhanced hardness decreased the deformation of sliding surface, consequently decreasing wear rate dramatically [ 84 ]. On the basis of these results, it can be concluded that carbide reinforcements, regardless of their fabrication method (in-situ or ex-situ) or particle scale (nano or micron), could be considered as a critical reinforcement type in the modification of both mechanical and tribological properties of HEAs.

sections.heading: Oxide-Based Fillers
paragraphs: In order to enhance the structural integrity and functional performance of HEAs, one of the most effective approaches is oxide dispersion strengthening (ODS) [ 85 ,  86 ]. Among various oxides, alumina has demonstrated significant potential as a reinforcement component. A clear indication was given by a study wherein hot-isostatically pressed CoCrFeMnNi-Al 2 O 3  nanocomposites displayed a considerable improvement in hardness and yield strength while avoiding the formation of undesirable phases. In fact, in this study, Al 2 O 3  reinforcement stayed stable and helped grain refinement effectively through the dispersion strengthening and dislocation pinning [ 87 ]. In another study, the dispersion of nanoscale Al 2 O 3  particles into a MA-SPS-fabricated Al 0.4 FeCrCoNi 1.2 Ti 0.3  HEA was reported. Based on their results, adding this reinforcement resulted in the formation of a dense composite microstructure consisting of dual face-centered cubic (FCC) and body-centered cubic (BCC) phases, with Al 2 O 3  particles uniformly distributed along grain boundaries and strongly bonded to the matrix. This oxide dispersion promoted considerable grain refinement and induced abundant deformation twinning within the FCC phase, which effectively hindered dislocation motion. Therefore, increasing fracture strength, hardness, and plastic strain was found to be the best manifestation of Al 2 O 3  effectiveness for improving both strength and ductility in HEA systems [ 88 ]. Several studies have validated the strengthening capability of oxides in HEAs. For example, in a study performed on Al 0.4 FeCrCo 1.5 NiTi 0.3  HEACs [ 89 ], the addition of nano Al 2 O 3 , enhanced the ultimate strength via activation of Orowan-type and load-transfer mechanisms. Likewise, it is reported that CoCrFeMnNi-Al 2 O 3 p composites [ 90 ] could achieve an optimal balance between strength and ductility using a proper amount of reinforcement. Consistent with these observations, in FeCoNiCrMn HEAs, nano-Al 2 O 3  strengthened the matrix through combined Orowan looping, dislocation interaction and thermal mismatch mechanisms. Moreover, among CrFeCuMnNi-based HEAs reinforced with varying Al 2 O 3  contents, 3 vol% Al 2 O 3  was identified as the optimum reinforcement level, exhibiting both the refinement of grains and the simultaneous enhancement of compressive strength and wear resistance, which can be attributed to the uniform dispersion of particles and Zener pinning effects. In this mechanism, the dispersed oxide particles could act as stable obstacles at grain boundaries, thereby restricting their movement during high-temperature processing such as sintering and hot forging. Grain growth could effectively be suppressed with this pinning action, as indicated by the average grain size deduction and the enhancement of high-angle grain boundaries. The consequent presence of fine-grained microstructure could enhance the load-carrying capacity of the composite as well as its wear performance. It is also crucial to note that oxide phases may also play a critical role in refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). Extensive research has been conducted on RHEAs [ 62 ,  91 ,  92 – 93 ]. For instance, the formation of fine in-situ Ti–(O, N) nanoprecipitates in NbTaTiV alloys can be attributed to the enhancement of strength and the improvement of stability at high temperatures [ 94 ]. In a complementary study, the formation of in-situ Al 2 O 3  in NbTaMoW-based composites resulted in the improvement of toughness [ 95 ]. In another study, Al 2 O 3  reinforcement was used in AlCoCrFeNi HEAs, which resulted in the enhancement of hardness and wear resistance, confirming its dual role in both mechanical strengthening and tribological stabilization.

Even though Al 2 O 3  was distinguished as the most famous and widely-explored oxide reinforcement in HEACs, many other oxides have displayed notable strengthening effects and remarkable potential for improving the performance of these alloys. This included yttrium oxide, which has been frequently considered as a reinforcement oxide in various studies [ 96 ]. A famous group of oxides, known as REO, are ceramics derived from lanthanides which exhibit unique properties such as high melting temperature, chemical reactivity and stable thermal properties [ 97 ]. REOs are frequently utilized in manufacturing as grain refiners, reducing elements and microstructural modifying agents simply due to their special electronic structures and affinity to react with contaminants and oxygen. Frequently-used REOs such as Y 2 O 3 , La 2 O 3 , and CeO 2  are ideal for metal matrix composites (MMCs) as they have exceptional hardness and thermodynamic phase stability. In fact, the main reason that REOs can improve the mechanical and thermal performance of recently-designed HEAs can be related to their role in pinning grain boundaries, hindering grain growth and strengthening interfacial bondings [ 98 ]. Collectively, these benefits have led to growing attention in employing REOs in HEACs [ 85 ,  99 ,  100 ,  101 ,  102 – 103 ]. As an example, in a study on Al 1.8 CoCrCu 0.5 FeNi HEAs, which was fabricated by MA followed by SPS, it is reported that Y 2 O 3  had a major effect on microstructural refinement and enhancement of hardness through the formation of solid-solution phase and grain-boundary strengthening [ 104 ]. Increase in hardness and elastic modulus observed after SPS consolidation, were primarily due to grain size reduction and solid-solution strengthening which was achieved during MA process. Likewise, Al 0.3 CoCrFeMnNi HEAs with 3 vol% Y 2 O 3  achieved a remarkable increase in compressive yield strength attributed to fine-grain formation and in-situ nano-oxide dispersions [ 105 ]. Comparable strengthening performance was also observed in CoCrFeNi HEAs, where uniformly distributed Y 2 O 3  nanoparticles produced high yield strength via coherent particle matrix interfaces and combined precipitation and dislocation strengthening [ 106 ]. Moreover, in CoCrFeNiMn-based HEAs reinforced with in-situ formed Y 2 O 3  nanoparticles, grain refinement and dispersion strengthening led to remarkable improvement in strength and creep resistance, with dislocation pinning identified as the dominant mechanism [ 107 ]. In another study, Y 2 O 3  was introduced into an NbTaTiV refractory HEA using MA and SPS. Although a slight reduction in fracture strain was observed at higher oxide contents, the presence of finely dispersed Y 2 O 3  and related oxide particles refined the grain structure and led to an obvious increase in compressive strength [ 108 ]. In other study, Al 0.3 CoCrFeMnNi HEA reinforced with Y 2 O 3  was fabricated by MA and SPS, the results showed a steady increase in strength as the oxide content was increased. The improvement was mainly linked to the formation of fine and stable oxide dispersions, which effectively hindered the movement of dislocations and strengthened the alloy via ODS mechanism [ 109 ]. Additional investigations studied the effect of nano-sized Y 2 O 3  addition on MA-SPS-fabricated Ni-rich HEA. It was reported that adding a certain amount of Y 2 O 3  (around 3% vol.) could increase the hardness and compressive strength. While higher amounts of Y₂O₃ might lead to the agglomeration of particles and subsequently restrict the improvement of mechanical properties due to inadequate densification [ 110 ].

Another popular oxide reinforcement group in HEACs can be transition metal oxides (TMO) such as Ti, Zr, Hf, etc. Among them, titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ), has widely been the subject of several research works for its potential to increase both mechanical and tribological properties. For instance, in a study performed on CrFeCuMnNi-based HEAs [ 20 ] synthesized through PM method, the addition of TiO₂ nanoparticles significantly enhanced hardness, strength, and wear resistance. It was reported that enhanced surface durability and lower friction could be due to the presence of a surface oxide film during sliding, which was another evidence indicating the importance of TiO₂ as reinforcement. Aside from TiO 2 , other forms of titanium oxides have also shown remarkable strengthening potential in HEA systems. For instance, in another study on PM-synthesized Ni 1.5 Co 1.5 CrFeTi 0.5  HEA [ 111 ], considerable enhancement of both strength and ductility was reported due to the presence of dispersed nano-sized titanium oxide along with coherent precipitates of Ni 3 Ti intermetallic phase. Increase of strength was mainly due to Orowan-type strengthening, as TiO 2  and Ni 3 Ti precipitates cannot be sheared by dislocations, consequently allowing them to bend around the barriers. This greater dislocation motion resistance can subsequently result in enhancing the deformation stress, boosting strength without decreasing ductility.

Zirconium oxide (ZrO₂) is another type of oxide reinforcement which has been widely investigated in HEAs. Two simultaneous investigations undertaken by the same research team employed ZrO 2  as a reinforcing agent in AlCoCrFeNi-based HEAs [ 112 ,  113 ]. Their findings revealed that the incorporation of ZrO 2  improved the morphology of particles, stabilized the presence of a dual FCC-BCC microstructure and simultaneously enhanced both hardness and wear resistance. This simultaneous enhancement could be due to the presence of hard ZrO₂ particles which not only reinforced both FCC and BCC phases, but also restricted plastic deformation at contact surface, consequently improving hardness and reducing material removal during sliding. Another study performed on refractory NbMoTaW systems [ 93 ], investigated the impact of ZrO₂ particles acting as reinforcement. In this study, refractory alloy was modified by the addition of nano-sized monoclinic ZrO 2  particles via PM technique, which resulted in significant grain refinement and concurrent enhancement of strength and ductility.

Another widely-reported oxide, hafnium oxide (HfO 2 ), was employed to modify the microstructure of PM-fabricated CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys [ 114 ]. It was also reported that the homogenous distribution of HfO 2  nanoparticles could remarkably enhance the hardness, compressive yield strength, and wear resistance. These improvements were primarily associated with uniform dispersion of reinforcements and grain boundary strengthening or Hall-Petch strengthening, alongside a major change in the dominant wear mechanism from severe to mild abrasive wear. As a matter of fact, when HfO 2  particles were incorporated into the alloy, they strengthened the surface by making it more resistant to damage, thereby reducing the possibility of significant cracking. As a result, the surface tended to wear down more gradually through tiny scratches and grooves instead of undergoing severe deformation, exactly consistent with the behavior of abrasive materials slowly grinding down a surface. In fact, stability in CoCrFeNi HEAs was achieved by inhibiting grain coarsening during prolonged annealing, maintaining around 84% of the original hardness through Sm/Cr-O phase formation [ 115 ].

sections.heading: HEA as Reinforcement Filler in MMCs
paragraphs: MMCs have received increasing attention in both academic and industrial-scale applications due to their unique properties which are experimentally inaccessible for conventional alloy systems [ 116 ,  117 ,  118 – 119 ]. Since the emergence of HEAs, the idea of using HEAs as reinforcements in MMCs has become a dominant design strategy for next-generation composites [ 51 ,  120 ,  121 – 122 ]. In fact, HEAs are gaining increasing attention as reinforcing components in composite systems due to their outstanding properties such as significant mechanical properties, great oxidation resistance, and even their stability at elevated temperatures. Many studies have been reported in this regard. Figure  5  depicts the effect of reinforcement type, using ceramic as reinforcement in traditional lightweight metal-matrix composites (LMMCs) compared with employing HEA fillers in modern ones. As represented in Fig.  5 (a), for conventional ceramic-reinforced composites, the reason for being vulnerable to failure could be poor interfacial bonding among reinforcement and matrix as well as visible crack propagation across their weak and fragile interface. In contrast, as presented in Fig.  5 (b), when HEA acted as reinforcement, their strong metallic bonding with the matrix can not only enhance load transfer, but also suppress crack formation, and most importantly result in the overall enhancement of strength and toughness. In Fig.  5 (c), the process of crack propagation in conventional alloys is compared with that in HEAs, as outlined earlier.

Fig. 5 A comparative graphical depiction of ( a ) conventional ceramic-reinforced LMMCs, ( b ) HEA-reinforced LMMCs, ( c ) the comparison of propagation of cracks in both conventional systems and HEAs design [ 118 ,  123 ]

Among various types of MMCs, aluminum matrix composite (AMC) is known as important research field in engineering [ 123 ,  124 ,  125 ,  126 ,  127 ,  128 ,  129 ,  130 ,  131 ,  132 ,  133 – 134 ]. Although pure Al alloys show desirable properties such as low density and great strength for structural engineering performance, they face challenges related to their limited tribological performance. To address this issue, innovative alloying strategies such as reinforcing Al-matrix with other particles including conventional ceramic fillers or even recently introduced HEA fillers have significantly improved their performance in multiple applications consisting of aviation, aerospace, and automotive industries [ 124 ,  135 ]. Among the studies conducted on AMCs modified by HEAs [ 125 ,  132 ,  136 ,  137 ], Wang et al. [ 125 ] investigated the enhancement of the properties of AMCs with CuZrNiAlTiW HEA as reinforcement. Their composite was fabricated by MA, followed by SPS. Based on their findings, the ball-milled HEA powder consisting of BCC solid solution phase showed an interesting core–shell-type microstructure which was associated with the achievement of significant overall compression performance. It has been reported that strength in Al-based systems with high-entropy oxides such as Cr 0.23 Mn 0.22 Fe 0.22 Co 0.19 Ni 0.13 O 4  was primarily attributed to the combined effects of Hall-Petch strengthening, dispersion hardening, ORS [ 138 ]. Moreover, ODS-AlCrFeNi composites reinforced with CoCrFeNiMn HEA powder (around 3 wt% of Y 2 O 3 ) demonstrated stable oxide formation (Y 4 Zr 3 O 12 ), an FCC to BCC phase transition, and improved strength through spinodal decomposition [ 139 ].

For lightweight structural magnesium (Mg) composites, many studies have been performed by various researchers [ 140 ,  141 ,  142 – 143 ]. Among them, Gopal et al. [ 140 ] worked on developing Mg matrix composite (MgMC) reinforced with novel FeCoCrNiMn HEA fabricated by PM. Considering the limitation of pure Mg, particularly its low hardness and wear resistance, various researchers have tried to solve this problem by the incorporation of other reinforcing elements. Meanwhile, HEAs have emerged as a promising candidate to serve as reinforcement for developing various lightweight composites. In fact, the application of HEA as reinforcement offered several benefits over traditional ceramic reinforcements. Conventional ceramic-reinforced composites previously suffered from imbalances in the thermal expansion coefficient, insufficient interfacial wettability and the limitation of low crystallization temperatures. In the context of utilizing HEAs as reinforcement, they not only show similar thermal expansion coefficients to metals, but also can exhibit phase transformation stability, thereby guaranteeing increased compatibility and performance durability. Another widely investigated category of MMCs, known as titanium matrix composites (TMCs), have been the focus of multiple studies [ 144 ,  145 ,  146 ,  147 ,  148 ,  149 – 150 ]. From a practical standpoint, classical TMCs commonly face issues, similar to other MMCs, mainly lack of a strong interfacial bonding among ceramic particles as reinforcements and titanium matrix as well as suffering from poor wettability, consequently resulting in the restriction of material flexibility and formability. In addition, appropriate dispersion of fine ceramic particles throughout the matrix during traditional thermomechanical processing becomes problematic for high volume fraction. The addition of HEAs particles serves as a solution by promoting direct alloying and firming MMC systems, which produce fundamentally strong interfacial bonding. In fact, by generating a multiphase structure consisting of FCC solid solution and σ phase in the diffusion zones and activating multiple strengthening mechanisms, this approach can significantly enhance mechanical properties, which involve achieving a balance between tensile strength and UTS [ 145 ].

Other widely used MMCs, Cu-based composites (CuMC), traditionally encounter limitations in strength, thermal stability and inherent imbalance among their conductive and mechanical properties. In fact, conventional reinforcements including ceramic particles that possess insufficient wettability and poor interface adhesion to copper matrix usually worsen these problems. In contrast, regarding HEAs-reinforced Cu-matrix composites, they show exceptional inherent strength, ductility and hardness, which can finally result in acceptable electrical conductivity while generating noticeably enhanced mechanical properties [ 151 ]. Many studies have focused on HEA-reinforced CuMC [ 151 ,  152 ,  153 ,  154 ,  155 ,  156 ,  157 – 158 ]. Within this framework, Zhang et al. [ 159 ] studied the influence of NbTaMoW HEA particles on Cu-6% Ag composites, fbricated by MA followed by SPS. In their study, the presence of HEAs resulted in the formation of a refined grain structure with a well-bonded interface with matrix. The obtained composite showed a considerable balance between mechanical and electrical properties. In CuMC, nanocrystalline TiZrNbTa HEAs (~ 10 nm) facilitated robust interfacial adhesion, efficient load transmission, and improved crack resistance, supported by fine particle dispersion and sintering stability [ 160 ].

sections.heading: Hybrid HEA-Filler Reinforcements
paragraphs: Among earlier investigations on hybrid reinforcements, Ezatpour et al. [ 141 ] studied magnesium matrix composites (MgMCs) reinforced with a mixture of HEA and CNT+GNPs. In fact, they reported that mixing 1% CNT + GNP with CoCrFeNiMoTi HEA resulted in the formation of the most refined grain structure with a well-dispersed reinforcement. Consequently, their design showed significant mechanical and tribological properties, a remarkable synergy of strength-plasticity, compared to Mg/HEA surface composites. Küçükelyas et al. [ 161 ] studied the increasing of electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness in carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites by means of CoCuFeNi HEA particles. They successfully fabricated HEA powder via MA and then mixed them with epoxy resin to make their final composites. Based on their findings, 10% HEA concentration had a homogeneous particle distribution without void compared to other concentrations. In fact, this optimized distribution improved its electrical conductivity and reflection-based shielding properties. Zhu et al. [ 162 ] worked on the development of lightweight HEA/N-doped carbon aerogel composites. In order to fabricate this advanced material, in-situ formation of FeCoNiCuMn HEA on 2D carbon substrate resulted in the generation of a composite aerogel with a hierarchical microstructure. The strategy of combining HEAs with lightweight carbon materials was implemented to overcome the high density and insufficient impedance matching traditional HEAs. In fact, addition of carbon could significantly reduce overall density while increasing electromagnetic loss mechanisms such as interfacial polarization and conductive loss. Putting all together, these materials are ideal candidates for protective applications in aerospace and advance electronics or even other highly-needed thermal management applications.

sections.heading: Hybrid Reinforcements
paragraphs: As a recent trend in materials engineering, introduction of hybrid reinforcements into a complex HEA matrix has also garnered significant attention [ 163 ]. Hybrid reinforcements are widely investigated as a result of their potential to provide both improved mechanical and functional performance, particularly under harsh or extreme service conditions. Regarding the production of industrial inert-anode applications for aluminum electrolysis, Qian et al. [ 164 ] fabricated more cost-effective high-entropy dodecaboride (HEDB) ceramic composites, named HEDB-Gd and HEDB-Sm, via combination of boron thermal reduction and SPS approaches. These materials have shown a chemically-inert and hard-cubic dodecaboride matrix with a minor hexaboride secondary phase, forming a three-dimensional boron network providing strong metallic conductivity and excellent corrosion resistance in molten cryolite salt. Subsequently, these HEDB composites can combine exceptional corrosion resistance, superior electrical conductivity and elevated hardness, making them promising candidates for designing low-cost and density anode applications. Several studies have been performed on HEA-MWCNTs composites, extensively used for microwave absorption applications, due to the importance of MWCNTs in enhancing electrical conductivity and increasing surface defect density. As a result, the incorporation of MWCNTs with HEA enhanced corrosion resistance and optimized impedance matching [ 165 ].

In the context of promising extreme-temperature structural materials for harsh environments such as hypersonic vehicles and advanced next-generation nuclear reactors, refractory metals including W, Ta, Mo, and Nb, together with their alloys mostly showing BCC structures, can be great choices due to their considerable ability to preserve superior high-temperature strength [ 166 ]. Many studies have been conducted on RHEAs and their application in composites [ 167 ,  168 ]. Among numerous studies on this topic, Wang et al. [ 169 ] conducted research on TiNiCuZrNbTa refractory HEA coatings using laser cladding and showed a neat microstructure and thereby excellent performance by the strategy of using multi tightly-bonded phases as reinforcements including TiNb, TiCuNi and Zr 14 Cu 51 . Moreover, the presence of metal oxides such as TiO 2 , ZrO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and Ta 2 O 5  allowed the formation of a protective oxide layer during wear. In fact, for critical applications such as aerospace copper alloy components, which need to deal with harsh environments or heavy loads, the presence of this complex microstructure dramatically improves the wear performance of the alloys making them promising candidates for future research. On the other hand, RHEAs are promising candidates for harsh environments simply because of their unique properties, including their resistance to high temperature, oxidation, corrosion, as well as their hardness or even special radiation resistance, as presented in Fig.  6 .
Fig. 6 Schematic diagram of the attractive features of RHEAs [ 170 ,  171 ]

In some studies, the type of employed filler could not be classified within any of the previously mentioned groups such as Ti boride [ 163 ,  172 ,  173 ,  174 ,  175 – 176 ], nitrides [ 177 ,  178 ,  179 – 180 ] or other borides [ 181 ,  182 ]. For instance, in a study performed by Wang et al. [ 183 ], TiB 2  was used as reinforcement in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1  eutectic HEA matrix. It was reported that the oxidation behavior of their alloy was significantly affected by Ti addition. In fact, at decreased sintering temperatures, an outer TiO 2  layer was formed due to the diffusion of Ti toward the surface. Conversely, at elevated sintering temperatures, the improvement of solid solution strengthening and higher lattice distortion could be attributed to higher solid solubility of Ti atoms. The dispersion of TiB 2  and its interfacial bonding with the matrix could subsequently impact the diffusion of oxygen and metal ions, thereby changing the oxidation mechanism and improving its oxidation resistance. In a study conducted by Gong et al. [ 184 ], porous Al x FeCrNi HEAs composite produced via reactive sintering contained in-situ NiAl-rich intermetallic as reinforcement. In fact, due to the shifting of matrix from FeCr-rich FCC (with low Al) to NiAl-rich B 2  (with high Al), a synergistic effect of ductility, strength and resistance to thermal shock was achieved. Moreover, these HEAs are ideal candidates for filter applications at elevated temperatures particularly in harsh environments, which can be mainly due to the enhancement of gas permeability through their porous structure. Similarly, Chang et al. [ 185 ] reported the fabrication of a RHEA with in-situ formed reinforcements through reactive sintering. They emphasized the critical role of TiC ceramic particles as uniformly dispersed reinforcement throughout the RHEA-based matrix. In fact, the formation of exothermic reactions between elemental powders can enhance the evolution of reinforcement phases, thereby increasing the ultimate mechanical properties of RHEA and their thermal properties. Notably, these materials are very suitable for structural applications in extreme thermal environments arising from their excellent performance at high temperatures, particularly above 1000  ° C.

Among various studies conducted on high-entropy carbide (HECA) [ 186 ,  187 ], Zhao et al. [ 188 ] produced ultrafine dual-phase (TiZrHfNbTa)C-SiC composite ceramics via in-situ reactive hot-pressing of silicon powders and nanoscale HECA. Moreover, they emphasized that (TiZrHfNbTa)C acts as matrix, while in-situ formed β-SiC serves as the strengthening phase, making these materials great candidates for advanced aerospace thermal protection and even extreme-environment structural components. Among the studies performed on in-situ formed reinforcements, Liu et al. [ 95 ] employed reactive sintering using a thermite reaction and SPS technique to fabricate a composite of NbTaMoW RHEA as the matrix with fine and uniformly distributed alumina particles as reinforcement. Due to their particular design, mechanical strength and fracture toughness were enhanced notably, while sustaining excellent thermal shock resistance. When it comes to extreme-environment applications such as hypersonic aerospace vehicles and elevated-temperature components in nuclear reactors, these materials can be promising alternatives for researchers. Recently, Youness et al. [ 189 ] fabricated Akermanite (AK) nanocomposites via MA + SPS, which were reinforced with several phases including silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4 ), HEA, and Ti 3 AlC 2  MAX. They emphasized that their composite showed significant mechanical strength, fracture toughness, electrical conductivity, and outstanding bioactivity confirming their great potential for load-bearing bone healing and replacement applications. In fact, their enhanced properties supported bone regeneration and implant integration with natural bone tissue.

With regard to special materials which are suitable for extreme-environment applications such as aerospace thermal protection and nuclear reactor linings as well as military applications, Wang et al. [ 190 ] employed MA followed by reactive SPS technique through the incorporation of ultrathin and flexible Ti 3 C 2  MXene layered sheets, acting as the reinforcement phase within a (Ti 0.2 Zr 0.2 Nb 0.2 Hf 0.2 Ta 0.2 )C 0.5 N 0.5  high-entropy carbonitride ceramic (HECNC) matrix. Their significant performance can be attributed to their superior mechanical and thermal stability. In another study, Yoon et al. [ 191 ] designed a radial gradient material combining Cu-based HEA and pure chromium (Cr) by means of hot isostatic pressing (HIP). They emphasized that this design could create a gradual compositional change from center-layered Cu-HEA to Cr at the outer layer, combining both irradiation resistance and corrosion protection for nuclear fuel cladding applications. This work indicated the notable potential of PM-HIP for the fabrication of advanced radial graded materials in extreme environments. In terms of designing special composites for high-speed machining tool applications, Sun et al. [ 192 ] developed a composite material with in-situ formed reinforcements through reactive sintering using a two-step SPS technique. The matrix consisted of (HfTaTiWZr)C HECA combined with a Co binder, while the reinforcements included hybrid multilayer graphene (MLG), MCNT, nano-sized VC/Cr 3 C 2 , and Al 2 O 3  particles. This composite also offered improved hardness, fracture toughness, and wear resistance. In terms of functionally graded ceramics, enabling the development of advanced ceramics suitable for cutting tool applications, wear-resistant parts, aerospace components, and even protective armor production, Zheng et al. [ 193 ] fabricated another HEC using in-situ formed ZrO 2  strengthening phases through reactive sintering of a two-step SPS method. In fact, a gradient distribution of dual toughening phases containing HECA- (HfNbTaTiZr)C- and ZrO 2  was fabricated within an Al 2 O 3  matrix, where this gradient reinforcement approach enabled the development of advanced ceramics suitable for applications such as cutting tools, wear-resistant parts, aerospace components, and protective armor. In another study, Hassan et al. [ 194 ] investigated the fabrication of (HfNbTaTiZr)B 2 –(HfNbTaTiZr)C high-entropy dual-phase ceramics, employing in-situ reinforcements formation through reactive sintering. In this system, the (HfNbTaTiZr)B 2  phase served as the reinforcement, while (HfNbTaTiZr)C phase acted as the matrix. These ceramics demonstrated improved flexural strength at both room and high temperatures, making them suitable for ultra-high temperature applications such as next-generation space vehicle components subjected to severe thermo-mechanical stresses. In terms of superior corrosion-resistant alloys designed for demanding marine applications, microstructural engineering can play a critical role. For instance, employing nanocrystalline-amorphous composites can combine chemical homogeneity and pit resistance of amorphous phases with the formation of a rapid passive film and enhancement of mechanical properties through the presence of nanocrystalline grains, granting the achievement of an optimal balance between the final mechanical performance and corrosion. In fact, the formation of eutectic and spinodal decomposition structures can result in reaching a better protection due to the stability of their surface films and preventing the occurrence of corrosion in specific regions. Moreover, these nano eutectic structures with nanoscale lamellar designs of alternating phases can provide a high-density network of phase boundaries which can promote compact and continuous passive films while activating crack deflection and repassivation under synergistic erosion-corrosion conditions. Through the optimization of passive film stability and inhibiting localized attack, these materials can achieve the controlling of phase distribution, coherent interfaces, and grain refinement to provide improved corrosion resistance suitable for applications in demanding erosion-corrosion environments [ 195 ].

sections.heading: Fundamentals of Strengthening Mechanisms
paragraphs: Considering the importance of strengthening mechanisms in HEA, each reinforcement can activate several mechanisms which can be dominant and play a decisive role in enhancing mechanical performance. Before discussing the details of each study, it is better to have a general overview of various strengthening mechanisms which have been discussed in HEAs so far. Many researchers have been worked on various strengthening mechanisms which can be activated in HEAs and HEACs [ 196 ,  197 ,  198 – 199 ]. Figure  8  depicts the six key widely-discussed mechanisms in HEAs. In solid solution strengthening, as shown in Fig.  8 (a), solute atoms dissolved in the matrix can result in lattice distortion, impeding further movement of dislocations. In fact, the presence of atoms with various sizes (interstitial, replacement with similar size or even replacement with larger radius) can produce localized stress fields, thereby increasing the ultimate strength as well as resistance to slip. Another famous mechanism, known as grain boundary strengthening or refinement strengthening mechanism, as shown in Fig.  8 (b), is known as a famous and important toughening mechanism. In this mechanism, the presence of reinforcement particles in matrix may result in pinning matrix grain boundaries, which can further limit grain growth. In fact, the presence of finer grains can more effectively hinder and block the motion of dislocations due to the misorientation of adjacent grains, thus increasing the ultimate strength of our composite via hindering the propagation of dislocations. Figure  8 (c) shows dual-phase strengthening mechanism. Due to the coexisting of both soft and hard phases, this mechanism can be useful for material as it can benefit from both the ductile deformation ability of the soft phase and the blockage of dislocation motion by the hard phase. This combination of behavior can result in a balance between strength and ductility. Figure  8 (d) shows dislocation strengthening mechanism which can contain both dislocation-cutting mechanism (depicted at top) and dislocation-bypass mechanism, known as Orowan looping (depicted at bottom). Dislocation-cutting mechanisms can happen when the tiny precipitations are formed coherently throughout the composite matrix. In fact, dislocations shear through the coherent precipitates and increase modulus, coherency and ordering strengthening. Another famous mechanism of dislocation, known as Orowan looping mechanism, takes place when the dislocation motion is blocked and bent around the precipitations, which can result in the formation of dislocation loops. In fact, due to this mechanism, the movement of dislocation requires applying higher forces, ultimately strengthening the alloy [ 196 ]. The twin boundary mechanism shown in Fig.  8 (e) illustrates the enhancements of nanoscale strength through the interactions of dislocations and twin boundaries. This occurs due to stress concentration at a twin boundary which is directly proportional to the applied shear stress and the number of accumulated dislocations. In fact, when the twinned layer is very thin, it can trap fewer dislocations, requiring a higher applied stress for dislocations to overcome these boundaries. Ultimately, twin boundaries act as obstacles to dislocation motion and serve as accumulation points for dislocations during large plastic deformation, consequently improving the mechanical properties of the material [ 198 ]. Load transfer strengthening, as depicted in Fig.  8 (f), is a well-known mechanism in composites where the applied load is transferred from the softer matrix material to the harder reinforcement particles. Since reinforcement particles have higher strength and stiffness, they bear a greater portion of the load under stress, decreasing stress on the matrix and enhancing the overall strength of the composite. In fact, this efficient load sharing between phases increases the mechanical performance of the material by hindering the premature deformation of the softer matrix [ 199 ].

Fig. 8 Schematic illustration of toughening and strengthening mechanisms in HEAs including: ( a ) solid solution strengthening; ( b ) grain boundary strengthening; ( c ) dual-phase strengthening combining strength and ductility, ( d ) dislocation strengthening including bypass and cutting [ 196 ], ( e ) Nanoscale twin boundary strengthening through interactions between dislocations and twin boundaries [ 198 ], ( f ) load transfer strengthening mechanism [ 199 ]

The schematic diagrams of some other responsible mechanisms crucial for achieving desired mechanical properties in HEAs and MMCs are presented in Fig.  9 . Figures  9 (a) and (b) also illustrate the strengthening and toughening mechanism of HEAs through fracture bridging and crack deflection. Crack bridging is a mechanism that occurs when reinforcements pass through fractured surfaces shortly after the creation of crack in matrix, thereby applying sealing stress to inhibit further crack propagation. During crack deflection, cracks can break away from its path and expand along the interfaces or pass through the barriers, subsequently enhancing strength through the absorption of fracture energy. Several common strengthening mechanisms for HEAs are also presented in Fig.  9 (c), including (i) solid solution strengthening, (ii) fine-grain strengthening, (iii) strengthening through dislocations, (iv) load transfer strengthening in composites, (v) dispersion strengthening, and (vi) phase transformation of Transformation-induced plasticity dual-phase high-entropy alloy (TRIP-DP-HEA). Solute atoms can induce lattice distortion finally leading to the occurrence of solid solution strengthening mechanism. The presence of fine-grain reinforcements can refine grain size and consequently increase ultimate strength, which is called fine grain strengthening mechanism. Another famous mechanism, known as dislocation strengthening, can occur by stopping further movement of dislocations, which is restricted by the entanglement of dislocations. Load transfer strengthening mechanisms can take place when composite matrix cracks. In this mechanism, the majority of load can be transferred to strong reinforcing particles, subsequently enhancing ultimate strength. A famous type of HEA, dual-phase HEA, is specifically designed for enhancing mechanical properties by having both superior strength and considerable toughness. Their improved performance can be achieved through TRIP effect, which includes stress-assisted phase transformation coming from the formation of a metastable phase. In fact, when a metastable phase (typically FCC) is subjected to a stress-assisted phase transformation, often into HCP phase, TRIP effect can be activated, ultimately resulting in improved mechanical performance. The formation and combined effects of stacking faults by enhancing interfacial density can serve as an obstacle to dislocation slip, finally promoting the strain hardening [ 200 ].

Figure  10  theoretically compares the approaches used for predicting yield stress. As shown in Fig.  10 (a), Hall-Petch relation was witnessed. It could be used for the prediction of the traditional yield stress (σ y ) of homogeneous materials, where the increasing of strength could be proportional to the inverse square root of grain size (d − 1/2 ) [ 201 ]. Figure  10 (b) depicts the concept of hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stress (σ HDI ). The technique of loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) could be used to estimate σ HDI . This could be represented as excess strengthening and strain hardening coming from the long-range back stresses generated by the pileups of dislocations at the interfacial region among soft and rigid zones. Figure  10 (c and d) a schematic of HDI strengthening which is a single-ended dislocation pileup model. This toughening mechanism can happen when hard zones stay elastic but soft areas can deform plastically, resulting in pileups of dislocations at their interfaces. As a result, a long-range internal stress can be formed which can block the further movement of dislocations and thereby enhance the final strength of material beyond simple mixing rule predictions. As can be seen in part (d), the ultimate yield stress (σ y ) which contains three parts, contributions from fine grains (referred as FGs), coarse grains (referred as CGs), and interface-strengthened CGs (referred as hardened CGs in yellow) [ 202 ].

sections.heading: Structure-Property Relationships in Reinforced HEAs
paragraphs: In order to gain a better understanding of the importance of microstructural effect, Fig.  11  shows how microstructure could be affected by wear, sintering, and shape reinforcement. It also shows the effects of these parameters on controlling the mechanical strength and stability of HEA-reinforced composites. Figure  11 (a) presents SEM secondary electron images captured by Li et al. [ 92 ] illustrating the subsurface structures of SiC 0  and SiC 0.2  alloys after undergoing wear tests at various temperatures. These results showed the effect of SiC on the microstructure and how it could improve wear resistance. As the temperature increased, wear trends might change, which confirmed that SiC enhanced the performance of HEAs at elevated temperatures. It emphasized the way by which SiC enhanced wear resistance and modified the subsurface response during sliding, thereby offering critical insights into their high-temperature performance. Figure  11 (b) presents the SEM-BSE results of B-15%F composites sintered at various temperatures (950–1100  ° C) obtained by Li et al. [ 139 ]. The results exhibited three distinct regions of the matrix, transition zone, and reinforcement. They reported that the structure of the composites changed from heterogeneity to more homogeneous phases as a result of enhanced diffusion. Subsequently, phase formation was influenced by spinodal decomposition, which enhanced mechanical properties.

In another work, Gao et al. [ 203 ] investigated FeCoCrNiAl HEAp and 7075Al matrix, producing specimens with 5–20 vol% reinforcement. Their findings showed that using 10 vol% HEAp achieved the best combination of hardness, strength, and durability. Their study particularly highlighted the importance of optimizing HEAp content for applications requiring good performance and lightweight materials. In this regard, a TEM image of HEAp-aluminum matrix interface is presented in Fig.  11 (c). An explanation of microstructural details, interface boundary and dislocation structures, that are essential for understanding the impact of particle reinforcement on the properties of composites, could be concluded from these results. The high-resolution HAADF micrograph presented in Fig.  11 (d) was taken from the work of Parizi et al. [ 68 ], displaying the separated and almost uniform dispersion of GNPs and CNTs within Cantor alloy matrix at a reinforcement content of 0.2 wt%. The improvement of mechanical properties and development of advanced composite materials with superior performance were directly influenced by this homogenous dispersion, which was crucial for effective load transfer. As could be seen from Fig.  11 (e), Ezatpour et al. [ 69 ] investigated the distribution and morphology of CrCoFeMnNi HEA particles with 0.2 wt% GNPs and CNTs in a high-magnification image. The successful dispersion of GNPs and CNTs within HEA powder indicated beneficial reinforcement placement, which was necessary for enhancing mechanical and wear properties. As reported by Pourghaz et al. [ 204 ], Fig.  11 (f) shows FESEM pictures of two samples, (i) CoCrFeMnNi HEA and (ii) HEA, with 0.2 wt% CNT added to it after SPS process. The results clearly showed that microstructures were very different. HEA had bigger carbide particles that were not arranged evenly, and the surface was more porous. In comparison, HEA and CNT samples showed smaller, more uniformly distributed precipitates and diminished porosity. This indicated that the addition of CNT improved the densification and overall microstructural consistency of the nanocomposite relative to unmodified HEA.
