sections.heading: Impacts of Reinforcement Type on Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: As discussed, the type of reinforcement plays a critical role in enhancing the final mechanical properties. An essential mechanical property that indicates the resistance of a material to wear and plastic deformation is hardness. Various reinforcements have been intentionally incorporated into HEA systems to considerably increase hardness. This could be achieved through mechanisms such as grain refinement, load transfer, solid-solution, and dispersion strengthening which are discussed elaborately in the next section. Figure  14  compares various reinforcement systems, containing the maximum achievable Vickers hardness or microhardness, represented by the upper limit of the reported values (including error bars) for each system, allowing a consistent evaluation of their strengthening potential. Hardness values exhibited a wide range from around 233 to 2192 HV, which is representative of unique strengthening mechanisms which can be activated by each reinforcement system. Based on the obtained results, the strongest combined effect of multiple carbides in impeding dislocation motion was seen in a (HfTaTiWZr)-based HEA reinforced with mixed carbides such as vanadium carbide (VC) and Cr₃C₂, obtaining the highest hardness of around 2192 HV. Similarly, the role of ceramic-carbide compounds in enhancing wear and deformation resistance was confirmed by aforementioned studies, which employed WC, borides such as ZrB 2 , TiB 2  or even a mixture of boride/nitride or boride/carbide, as their reinforcement. In systems reinforced with TiO and Al 2 O 3 , intermediate hardness levels were observed, ranging from 467 to 999 HV. Oxide and boride particles were responsible for improving the grain boundary stability and Orowan strengthening. Although employing oxides or various phases such as Intermetallic, σ, Lave or even Al 3 Ti phases can usually increase hardness properly, but it might reduce ductility. In contrast, carbonaceous reinforcements such as CNTs and GNPs exhibited low and moderate hardness values, ranging from around 426 to 774 HV which were mainly lower than carbides or borides. This could be attributed to their exceptional inherent strength, despite limited interfacial bonding. In general, the results indicated that hybrid ceramic-carbide reinforcements and oxide dispersion-strengthened systems exhibited outstanding hardness performance, making them appropriate for high-temperature and wear-resistant HEA applications.

Fig. 14 Comparison of maximum achievable hardness or microhardness (HV) considering the effects of different reinforcement types in HEAs and corresponding reference for each of them is indicated inside the figure

Figure  15  compares the mechanical properties of various reinforced HEAs, with special focus on the ultimate compressive strength (UCS) and compressive yield strength (CYS). To compare the potential of various reinforcement systems and identify the most suitable choice based on application requirements, similar to hardness/microhardness, maximum achievable CYS and UCS are represented here by the best reported combinations for each system. This illustration serves to guide the design of balanced properties or prioritize a higher amount of a specific property based on customized application. Figure  15 (a) clearly shows the impact of choosing various types of HEAs as reinforcements on CYS. Among various systems, ODS-CoCrFeNiMn HEA showed a considerable CYS value of around 2688 MPa due to the presence of finely dispersive Y 2 O 3 /Ti/Zr nanoparticles, which can serve as dislocation pinning centers causing grain boundaries refinement. The findings also confirmed that employing either mixed or complicated oxides such as Ta 2 VO 6  showed the significantly high amount of CYS, with values of around 2612 MPa. The high stiffness and strong interfacial bonding of TiO and Al 2 O 3 -based reinforcements were contributing factors in their strength, ranging from 1500 to 2075 MPa.

Carbides such as TiC or Ti (C, N) were also located at top of list. Orowan strengthening and particle refinement were two mechanisms which enabled carbide and hybrid reinforcements, such as Hf, Ta, Ti, W, and Zr reinforced with VC and Cr₃C₂, to achieve the maximum hardness levels of up to 2192 HV and a broad range of yield strengths ranging from 698 to 2100 MPa. CNTs and GNP reinforcements are forms of carbon nanostructures that provide moderate enhancement, less than ceramic, with yield strengths ranging from 702 to 1697 MPa, despite the fact that interfacial adhesion issues might limit their efficiency. CYS results showed that ODS and ceramic nanoparticle reinforcements improved the initial resistance to plastic deformation in HEACs the most, while carbon-based reinforcements only improved slightly to a moderate degree. The results also indicated the important role of hybrid reinforcements such as the mixture of carbide and oxide or intermetallics, which seems to provide a balance of hardness and toughness.

The UCS presented in Fig.  15 (b) provides further illustration of the significant influence of reinforcement type on the mechanical performance of HEACs. The findings confirmed that oxides such as ZrO 2  or complex oxides such as ODS, Ta 2 VO 6 , Al 3 Ti intermetallics possessed the highest amount of UCS. As reported by Zhu et al. [ 213 ], HEAs reinforced with ZrO 2  showed the highest amount of UCS, with the value of around 3759 MPa. In terms of employing alumina or ODS systems, UTS values between 1935 and 3489 MPa were reported. This could be attributed to the presence of homogeneous dispersed oxide particles, which efficiently hindered dislocation motion and could stabilize grain boundaries during deformation. Moreover, reinforcements such as TiO and TiC/TaC showed proper UCS values (2893 to 1906 MPa), which were mainly because of their role in improving the interfacial bonding and synergistic strengthening from load transfer and solid-solution processes. However, carbon-based reinforcements such as graphene and CNTs only slightly increased UCS (between 1914 and 2510 MPa), indicating their limited load transfer at high strains. Despite their ability to disperse stress, their nanoscale reinforcements were restricted by weakened interface adhesion. Boride, carbide, and intermetallic reinforcements obtained intermediate strengths 1800 to 2710 MPa effectively achieving a balance between strength and ductility. Overall, UCS trends verified that the ODS and hybrid reinforcements achieved through microstructural refinement and dislocation immobilization were the best ways to maximize the ultimate compressive strength of HEACs. The most efficient reinforcements for enhancing compressive strength in HEACs were oxide (ODS) and hybrid (such as mixture of oxide and carbide), as demonstrated by both CYS and UCS trends. Carbonaceous reinforcements, on the other hand, only provided modest to moderate improvements.

Fig. 15 ( a ) Maximum achievable compressive yield strength and corresponding reference for each of them is indicated inside the figure, ( b ) Maximum achievable ultimate compressive strength for various reinforcements and corresponding reference for each of them is indicated inside the figure

As a conclusion, carbides or boride seem to provide the highest hardness, while oxides, ODS and intermetallics seem to perform better in terms of UCS. At the same time, a mixture of ODS/oxides and carbide/nitride can provide a better CYS. In terms of reaching a balanced performance regarding the combination of hardness and toughness, hybrid reinforcements such as mixture of oxides, carbides, and intermetallics can be the best candidate. The best choices for future HEA design can be hybrid reinforcements or a mixture of multiphase materials which can activate various strengthening mechanisms simultaneously. ODS-reinforced and ceramic-reinforced composites as well as high-strength metallic and ceramic composites also have attracted great attention similar to HEAs which could be due to their outstanding mechanical properties. Based on the findings of various researchers, main reinforcing mechanisms such as grain boundary refinement, precipitation strengthening, crack deflections, and particle reinforcement can enhance the mechanical stability and structural integrity of these materials, thereby allowing them to be suitable for operation in harsh environments. In order to fabricate advanced materials for cutting tools, nuclear energy, and aerospace industries that need exceptional performance in challenging environments, it is important to understand their microstructural properties and reinforcing mechanisms, which are discussed in next section.

sections.heading: Comparison of Reinforcement Effects and their Strengthening Mechanism
paragraphs: By using different types of reinforcement, complicated microstructures and higher configurational entropy of HEAs could be used to optimize their mechanical performance. Reinforcements could be categorized according to their specific features and the mechanisms through which they improve material properties. The incorporation of CNTs and GPNs in HEAs, synthesized through MA and SPS, presented major potential for improving mechanical properties among carbon-based reinforcements. This field is receiving substantial attention from research communities. Torabi Parizi et al. [ 68 ] showed that the incorporation of hybrid reinforcements, GNPs and CNTs, remarkably enhanced the mechanical properties of HEAs. Specifically, 0.2 wt% GNPs and CNTs hybrid reinforcement improved microhardness from 490 to 540 HV, increased compressive yield strength from 1332 to 1697 MPa, and enhanced overall mechanical performance. In another study performed by Ezatpour et al. [ 69 ], the same reinforcements were used to enhance the mechanical properties of HEAs by reducing agglomeration and optimizing nanoscale distribution to improve microhardness and wear resistance. They found that the presence of second-phase reinforcements might enhance toughness through better stress transfer and resistance to cracking. Furthermore, refining microstructure by using MA and SPS further boosted performance, highlighting the importance of hybrid carbonaceous reinforcements in advancing HEAs for structural applications. Pourghaz et al. [ 204 ] found that the addition of CNT into CoCrFeMnNi HEA enhanced its structural integrity, strength, hardness and corrosion resistance, which were related to particle refinement and increase of dislocation density. Liu et al. [ 66 ] modified CoCrFeNiMn HEA using GNPs as reinforcement for the laminated microstructure of CoCrFeNiMn HEA, inspired by “brick-mortar” of nacre. Its layered microstructure promoted dislocation movement, twinning, and fracture deflection, improving strength and ductility. They reported that their laminated HEA could achieve compressive strength of 2177 MPa and tensile strength of 673 MPa. In contrast, GNPs-HEA composites showed improved properties with compressive strength of 2530 MPa and tensile strength of 826 MPa, along with better ductility. In fact, GNPs increased grain boundary area and controlled dislocation dynamics, enabling energy absorption and crack deflection, resulting in strong, yet ductile composites. Jialin Sun et al. [ 192 ] investigated the mechanical properties and reinforcement strategies of high-entropy cemented carbide materials, with an emphasis on using nano-reinforcements such as MLG and multiwall CNTs. In their study, they performed a two-step SPS process in order to show that when HEAs were used as reinforcements in ceramic composites, it was a great balance that could achieve hardness and fracture toughness compared to conventional tungsten carbide-cobalt composites. In fact, by controlling residual stress while activating strengthening or toughening mechanisms such as crack deflection, mechanical performance could be significantly enhanced. The goal was to offer high-entropy cemented carbides and ceramic systems specially for applications demanding wear resistance and high-speed machining.

Carbides are hard ceramic materials composed of carbon and less electronegative elements, known for their high melting points and wear resistance. Carbide reinforcements such as TiC [ 76 ,  232 ,  274 ], SiC [ 26 ,  92 ,  251 ,  255 ], NbC [ 257 ] WC [ 262 ,  267 ,  278 ,  281 ] are becoming more popular in HEAs. These reinforcements improved mechanical and thermal properties by grain refinement and enhanced resistance to wear and oxidation. Their applications are extensive and range from aerospace and automotive to industrial tooling fields [ 76 ,  92 ,  281 ,  282 ]. In a study performed by Li et al. [ 92 ], the impacts of SiC ceramic nanoparticles on the microstructure and tribological performance of Al 0.8 TiVNbNi 0.2  REHA were investigated. Based on their findings, SiC nanoparticles induced in-situ reactions which could result in the formation of TiC and Nb 5 Si 3  phases, thereby enhancing microhardness. The incorporation of SiC increased the tribological properties of this alloy over a wide temperature range (from RT to 800 °C), consequently achieving a wear rate reduction (more than 10 times) at 500 °C. It was also reported that at temperatures above 800 °C, wear mechanism was changed from abrasive to oxidative, with SiC becoming more resistant to softening and oxidation. In fact, the formation of SiO 2  oxides was enhanced at elevated temperatures, which could improve the uniformity and density of formed tribo-layer enhancing its ultimate wear resistance. This study indicated the promising role of SiC particles as suitable candidate for HEAs, especially for elevated-temperature wear applications. In another research performed by Yim et al. [ 76 ], TiC nano-particles were added into CoCrFeMnNi HEA resulting in a significant enhancement in mechanical properties. Their study showed that this addition decreased average grain size, which subsequently enhanced compressive yield strength and compressive fracture strength. The increased mechanical performance could be attributed to the presence of various strengthening mechanisms, including grain boundary strengthening, dispersion strengthening coming from TiC particles, and a notable enhancement of dislocation density during deformation. Their results also showed the promising role of TiC-reinforced HEACs for applications requiring high strength and ductility simultaneously. In a study by Chen et al. [ 282 ], TiC-Fe 24 Ni 24 Co 24 Mn 18  high-entropy composite exhibited outstanding mechanical and magnetic properties due to its unique microstructure and in-situ formed TiC nanoparticles. In fact, a heterogeneous microstructure with ultra-fine and micro-sized FCC grains alongside nanosized TiC particles was found after fabrication. Furthermore, it has been found that strengthening mechanisms, such as grain boundary strengthening, dispersion strengthening aided by TiC, and HDI strengthening, could significantly improve yield strength. At the same time, composite material revealed a low coercivity of approximately 100.5 A/m and high tensile yield strength of about 1167 MPa, followed by a total elongation of approximately 5.0%. This combination indicated a favorable balance between strength and ductility, offering it as a possibly appropriate candidate for advanced material applications. Wang et al. [ 281 ] examined microstructural modifications occurring during the heated deformation of a CoCrFeMnNi HEA containing 5% carbon. They discovered that carbides such as M 23 C 7  and M 23 C 6  were formed during processing and significantly improved hardness and strength. In fact, these carbides enhanced microstructural stability and resistance to dislocation movement, making the alloy competitive with conventional steel tools. They also reported that further refinement of carbide structures could be suggested for industrial performance improvement. In another research by Zhao et al. [ 82 ], (Hf 0.2 Nb 0.2 Ta 0.2 Ti 0.2 Zr 0.2 )N high-entropy nitrides were fabricated by SPS and reinforced with SiC w . The microstructural analysis confirmed enhanced densification and uniformity of their microstructure, with whisker bridging, pull-out, and crack deflection mechanisms contributing to fracture toughness. As a result of these microstructural features, cutting performance and tool durability as well as the wear resistance and mechanical properties were enhanced.

In order to enhance resistance to oxidation and corrosion as well as the mechanical strength of HEAs, researchers have widely used another popular group of reinforcement, known as REOs [ 105 ,  139 ,  206 ,  211 ,  283 ]. In fact, REOs can enhance the adhesion of oxide layers to the alloy matrix, thereby reducing fracturing at elevated temperatures. Rao et al. [ 211 ] studied the effect of the addition of Y 2 O 3  to AlCoCrFeNi HEAs, produced via mechanical alloying and SPS. They reported that the microstructure remained stable mainly due to the high melting point of Y 2 O 3  particles, which prevented phase transformation and grain growth during SPS. The findings also indicated that greater amounts of Y 2 O 3  could enhance mechanical properties via particle size strengthening and dislocation pinning. These findings indicated the promising role of Y 2 O 3  specially for high-strength and durable applications. In another study performed by Gwalani et al. [ 105 ], the addition of Y 2 O 3  into Al 0.3 CoCrFeMnNi HEA via MA and SPS was investigated. They reported that the employment of nano-dispersoids led to a considerable enhancement of yield strength, increasing from 979 to 1759 MPa. In addition, they performed a microstructural study to evaluate grain refinement and dispersion strengthening. Their findings showed that Y₂O₃ could be consider as an effective reinforcement to make HEAs more durable, which might also help future development in materials science [ 105 ]. Peng et al. [ 283 ] also investigated the role of Y 2 O 3  in the presence of Ti and Zr to generate evenly distributed oxide reinforcement in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Their research was all about using PM to increase the microstructural and mechanical properties. They also reported that the presence of Ti and Zr resulted in grain refinement with enhancing density of nanoscale oxides, finally reaching better hardness and compressive yield strength, due to the activation of Orowan strengthening mechanism. In general, this approach using Y 2 O 3  achieved optimal hardness and strength where alloy contained both Ti and Zr. The microstructure and mechanical properties of CrFeNi-based MEAs and HEAs containing YO₃ produced by MA and SPS were investigated by Peng et al. [ 206 ]. The fabricated alloys showed high-density nanoscale Y 4 Zr 3 O 12  oxides and a single FCC matrix with minimal presence of BCC phases. Their findings showed that grain refinement and solid solution strengthening significantly improved hardness and strength, while nanoscale oxides promoted Orowan strengthening and grain boundary pinning. An increase in principal elements led to larger grains and reduced hardness, highlighting the importance of microstructural control in optimizing alloy performance. As discussed before, among important categories of reinforcements, oxides play a critical role in enhancing the mechanical properties of HEAs. Among various researchers, Li et al. [ 139 ] examined the mechanisms of strengthening in oxide dispersion-enhanced CoCrFeNi HEA and determined the key factors enhancing their mechanical properties. These mechanisms included grain-boundary, dislocation, precipitation, and ODS. Based on Hall-Petch effect, yield strength of ODS-CCFN was increased as the particles became finer and that dislocation densities had a significant impact on the overall strength of materials. The addition of precipitates such as Cr 7 C 3  and Cr 2 O 3  let Orowan bypass mechanism perform better and enhanced composite yield strength. In fact, the presence of nano-scale oxide particles such as Y 2 Hf 2 O 7  created additional barriers to dislocation movements. These mechanisms collectively and simultaneously improved the mechanical performance of the alloys, consequently rendering them suitable for high-performance applications. A strong BCC-structured ODS-AlCrFeNi matrix and flexible FCC-structured ODS-CoCrFeNiMn reinforcement could bring a balance among strength and ductility to improve the ultimate mechanical performance. In fact, microcracks could be decreased by using homogeneous reinforcement, strain mismatch, and ODS. This research also indicated the potential of HEAC for applications requiring strength and ductility. In recent studies, Dingbo Sun et al. [ 284 ] worked on the fabrication of heterostructured ODS-FeCrAl composites reinforced with FCC-structured ODS-CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy particles. By controlling reinforcement amount, the microstructure was refined, showing a transition layer and an improved phase distribution. This layer showed that the strength and ductility of the material was improved. Composites also displayed enhanced mechanical performance as a result of reinforcement hardening and hetero-deformation mechanisms, making them promising candidates for nuclear applications. The addition of transition metals Ti, Zn, Fe, Mn, Ni, Cr, Co and Sc as oxide reinforcements into HEA such as NbMoTaW [ 93 ], (CoCrFeNi) 80 Mn 10 Ti 10  [ 285 ], CoCrFeNiTa [ 286 ] and AlCrFeNi [ 34 ] greatly enhanced the final mechanical performance. Mechanisms such as solid-solution strengthening, which prevent dislocation movement, along with robust metallic bonding and higher melting points, contribute to the enhanced strength and durability of these metals. In fact, thermal stability and ductility could be enhanced by using transition metals, which are critical for applications requiring good performance at elevated temperatures. HEAs are great candidates for advanced technical applications because of their excellent oxidation and corrosion resistance.

Among various studies in this filed, Zong et al. [ 93 ] conducted research on the strengthening mechanisms of NbMoTaW RHEAs reinforced with nano-sized m-ZrO 2  ceramic particles. They noticed that several critical mechanisms could contribute to the improvement of mechanical properties of these alloys. This included lattice strengthening, which was a consequence of the inherent frictional stress within NbMoTaW lattice; Grain boundary strengthening, which was a result of the refinement of grain size through the incorporation of m-ZrO 2  particles; and Orowan strengthening, in which the presence of ceramic particles impeded dislocation movement. Additionally, the strength of alloy was further improved by solid-solution reinforcement from interstitial atoms. Li et al. [ 285 ] investigated an ultrafine-grained (CoCrFeNi) 80 Mn 10 Ti 10  alloy enhanced with TiO nanoparticles produced by spark plasma sintering and mechanical alloying. They determined that the main processes of strengthening were dislocation interactions, grain boundary strengthening, Orowan strengthening from TiO particles, and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortions. With yield strength of 1500 MPa, strength of 2700 MPa, and strain of 36%, a high-performance alloy with outstanding strength and ductility was produced by adding Ti. In another research by Tang et al. [ 286 ], the strengthening mechanisms of CoCrFeNiTa HEAs were investigated, highlighting key factors contributing to their mechanical properties. Fine grain sizes in the supersaturated FCC and Laves phases enhanced strength by increasing grain boundary density, obstructing dislocation movement. They reported that the addition of Tantalum (Ta) to CoCrFeNiTa HEA improved strength via various strengthening mechanisms. This could be due to the big atomic size of Ta, inducing a lattice distortion, which could promote solid solution strengthening mechanism. As a result, it could stimulate the strengthening through the precipitation of nano-sized Ta, thereby effectively hindering dislocation motions. The presence of more rigid Co 2 Ta Laves phase further strengthened load-carrying capacity. They also reported that the presence of transition metals Co, Cr, and Ni could play a significant role in the stability of solid solutions and ultimate enhancement of mechanical properties. Employment of various kinds of transition metal oxides as reinforcements in HEAs has also gained significant interest among researchers [ 287 ]. A related study in this field was reported by Oke et al. [ 34 ] on the reinforcing mechanisms of TiO 2 -reinforced AlCrFeNi HEACs, discovering the critical parameters which could improve mechanical properties. Dispersion of TiO 2  addition could result in final strengthening which also consequently enhanced hardness and deformation resistance by hindering dislocation movement. Furthermore, Hall-Petch effect activated by TiO 2  particles induced refinement, while simultaneous diffusion of Ti and O into BCC and B 2  phases produced solid solutions, resulting in further enhancement of strength. The study highlighted the role of transition metals in changing microstructure and mechanical properties, thereby enhancing the overall performance of HEACs as well as stabilizing the predicted phases.

Another popular type of oxide is alumina [ 88 ,  89 – 90 ]. It is reported that this type of reinforcement could significantly enhance hardness and wear resistance due to its exceptional hardness and ability to uniformly distribute stress through load transfer from the matrix to alumina particles. The role of alumina in promoting grain refinement has been explored by many researchers. In this regard, Dai et al. [ 90 ] investigated Al 2 O 3 /CoCrFeMnNi composites. The refinement of grain structure could be achieved due to the presence of nano- Al 2 O 3  particles. It can result in an increase of yield strength by means of solid solution strengthening mechanism, grain boundary strengthening, dislocation, and Orowan strengthening mechanism. The formation of a heterogeneous microstructure increased the strength and ductility of composites containing coarse and ultrafine regions. Although moderate nano-Al 2 O 3 p content might improve properties, it was reported that excessive amounts caused agglomeration and subsequently affected ductility. In this study, Al 2 O 3 p referred to alumina nano-sized particles which were used as reinforcement in Al 2 O 3 /CoCrFeMnNi composites. In general, nano-Al 2 O 3 p enhanced HEA efficacy. In another study by Zhang et al. [ 94 ], an oxide-reinforced NbTaTiV RHEA with Al 2 O 3  was synthesized using MA and SPS. It exhibited excellent ductility and ultra-high yield strengths of 2075 MPa at room temperature and 690 MPa at 1000 °C. Solid-solution strengthening from Al and dispersed Ti-(O, N) particles were essential for their exceptional properties, particularly at high-temperature RHEAs. Yang et al. [ 89 ] found that adding nano-Al 2 O 3  to Al 0.4 FeCrCo 1.5 NiTi 0.3  HEA improved microstructure by enhancing nanoscale twins and deformation twinning. This increased yield strength to 2.05 GPa and compressive strength to 2.14 GPa, but diminished ductility. They mentioned that stress-strain curves demonstrated that serrated yielding and fracture were due to intergranular and cleavage mechanisms. In fact, in this study, MA and SPS improved the strength of alloys by enhancing interface bonding. Meanwhile, Yang et al. [ 88 ] investigated Al 2 O 3 -reinforced HEACs (Al 0.4 FeCrCoNi 1.2 Ti 0.3 ) produced through SPS and MA. The addition of Al 2 O 3  led to a good hardness (around 743 HV), plastic strain of 20%, and outstanding strength of around 2250 MPa. Solid solution effects, nanoscale Al 2 O 3 , and deformation twins that prevented dislocations were the primary causes of strengthening. These results confirmed the potential of these composites for high-performance and aerospace applications.

The microstructure of (NbTaTiV) BCC/Ti-C-O composite fabricated by Fu et al. [ 288 ] is represented schematically in Fig.  16 (a). Their microstructural investigations confirmed the formation of a dual-phase structure, including in-situ uniform dispersion of Ti-C-O particles as reinforcements and BCC phase of NbTaTiV alloy as matrix. In fact, these scattered Ti-C-O particles located at grain boundaries and within grains served as reinforcing agents. This arrangement could be the reason for its improved mechanical properties, including enhanced strength and resistance to deformation. Furthermore, they evaluated strengthening mechanisms such as solid-solution strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, and Orowan strengthening mechanism. In fact, Orowan strengthening mechanism plays critical role in reinforcing rigid Ti-C-O particles that can impede dislocations. Moreover, enhanced strength is achieved by the presence of fine grains, which create additional grain boundaries to further restrict the movement of dislocations. Moreover, distortion due to the presence of carbon in matrix can also hinder dislocations, consequently contributing to its outstanding mechanical properties, especially at elevated temperatures. The microstructure of the bulk Fe 24 Ni 24 Co 24 Mn 18  HEC modified with TiC is schematically presented in Fig.  16 (b). As was seen from the figure, three distinct regions were recognized: micro-sized grains (denoted as B), ultra-fine grains (represented as C), and nano-sized TiC particles. While larger grains contributed to strength through grain boundary effects, ultra-fine grains and uniformly distributed TiC nanoparticles increased strength through dispersion strengthening and microstructural stability. A heterogeneous microstructure was created by the combination of various particle sizes and nano reinforcements, which thereby enhanced the mechanical and magnetic properties of the final material. Moreover, it was found that its considerable mechanical performance could be attributed to the critical role of HDI strengthening mechanism, as the interactions among different microstructural regions could facilitate work hardening. These synergistic mechanisms were able to maintain excellent ductility and notably low coercivity, reaching a high yield strength of around 1167 MPa [ 282 ]. A comprehensive analysis of the strengthening mechanisms in HENCs tool materials which happened during crack propagation was performed by Zhao et al. [ 82 ], as presented in Fig.  16 (c). Part (i) of this figure illustrates the elemental analysis of crack extension, with a focus on the role of SiC W  through pull-out mechanisms and tensile fracture. Crack propagation is depicted in section (ii), indicating the essential role of microstructural features on promoting and hindering cracks development. Part (iii) illustrates toughening mechanisms, which included whisker pull-out, bridging, and crack deflection. These mechanisms explained how SiC W  reinforced ceramic matrix through crack bridging and whisker pull-out. Furthermore, whisker pull-out mechanism started when these fibers were pulled out from the matrix during cracking, which led to considerable energy absorption that retarded crack development. Successful application of SiC W  in enhancing the fracture toughness of HENCs was demonstrated by significant improvement in the mechanical characteristics of the materials brought about by these collective mechanisms. The microstructure and mechanical properties of ODS multi-principal element alloys, specifically ODS-CrFeNi, ODS-CoCrFeNi, and ODS-CoCrFeNiMn, were investigated by Peng et al. [ 206 ], Fig.  16  (d), which is brought from their work, illustrates the precipitation behaviors of nanoscale oxides in ODS CrFeNi-based multi-principal element alloys, including ODS-CrFeNi, ODS-CoCrFeNi, and ODS-CoCrFeNiMn. They reported that the mechanical properties of ODS-CrFeNi were improved by the increased density of nanoscale oxides, which was achieved through precipitation strengthening. Conversely, the addition of elements such as Co and Mn to ODS-CoCrFeNi and ODS-CoCrFeNiMn resulted in an increase in the size of the oxides, with simultaneous decrease in their number density. This was due to the reduced solubility of Y, Zr, and O in the Cr rich BCC phase. The research identified three strengthening mechanisms: solid solution strengthening, grain boundary strengthening facilitated by nanoscale oxides, and precipitation strengthening that impeded dislocation movement. The compressive yield strength and hardness of ODS-CrFeNi were the highest, suggesting that it had the potential to be developed into a high-performance alloy.

Figure  17  presents various microstructural features and strengthening mechanisms in some advanced alloys and composites, investigated by various researchers. The microstructure of an ODS-AlCrFeNi alloy and an ODS composite were examined by Li et al. [ 205 ] to determine their effects on micro-crack behavior during deformation, as seen in Fig.  17 (a). The figure depicts the final influence of prior particle boundaries on the strength and ductility of ODS-reinforced HEA before and after adding the reinforcement. Before adding the reinforcements, as presented in sections (i), (ii) and (iii), it was shown that prior particle boundaries (PPBs) specially could form among solidified powders after MA and SPS processing. During deformation, the propagation of microcracks could simply happen along PPBs. As a result, the final strength and ductility of the product could be deteriorated. In contrast, after adding ODS particles - as shown in sections (iv), (v) and (vi) - the homogenous distribution of ODS particles could be observed. In fact, during SPS, a transition region was formed due to the mutual diffusion of Al from the matrix and Co/Mn from reinforcement. This formed transition region could consequently enhance bonding as the temperature of sintering enhanced. Homogenous distribution of ODS as reinforcement interrupted continuous PPBs and therefore, the formation and propagation of microcracks was inhabited. Finally, the presence of these ODS reinforcement resulted in considerably enhancement in both strength and ductility of the final composite. Figure  17 (b) which is reported by Sun et al. [ 192 ], illustrates different strengthening mechanisms of functionally graded high-entropy cemented carbide. As it was seen in section (i), the propagation of a branching crack on fracture surface after performing single edge notched beam test was presented. Sections (ii) and (ii’) depict the effects of using a hybrid multilayer graphene (MLG) and multiwall CNT (MCNT) on crack growth hindering which could be due to crack branching and bridging mechanisms. Furthermore, high amount of Co in central and bonding layers, as could be seen in sections (iii), (iii’), (iv) and (iv’), could be considered as a critical factor decreasing energy for the propagation of cracks via the formation of microcracks or branching cracks, consequently enhancing its final fracture toughness. Figure  17 (c) shows critical function in the formation of powder morphology during ball milling (BM) process. At high milling speeds, the particles underwent substantial mechanical deformation due to the presence of friction among the milling media and the particles, which finally resulted in the formation of flattened, plate-like shaped particles. In fact, the enhancement of powder microstructure and promotion of major plastic deformation could be attributed to the presence of localized stress created by increased frictional forces. The formation of a fine, uniform powder which was crucial for afterward sintering can be considered as advantage of this process. As a result, friction influenced both powder properties and particle morphology, which were crucial for the production of high-performance materials. Moreover, Dai et al. [ 90 ] reported several strengthening mechanisms in their study which contributed to grain boundary, dislocation, solid solution and also the presence of second phase strengthening. In accordance with Hall-Petch effect, smaller grain sizes resulted in grain boundary strengthening and lattice strain caused by atomic size variations resulted in solid solution strengthening. Interactions within the matrix resulted in dislocation strengthening, while second phase strengthening, particularly from rigid nanoscale particles such as Al 2 O 3 , enhanced mechanical properties through Orowan strengthening mechanisms. The mechanical properties of the composites were substantially enhanced by these collective mechanisms.

Figure  17 (d), reported by Sun et al. [ 284 ], exhibits the strength-ductility coupling mechanism in heterostructure composites. In general, this study aimed to present heterostructure strategy to obtain strength-ductility synergy in FeCrAl alloys and CoCrFeNiMn composites reinforced with ODS. For critical applications such as the materials used in advanced nuclear reactors, reaching outstanding-performance materials is essential. Two important strengthening mechanisms, i.e., HDI and strain hardening, can significantly contribute to performance enhancement. In fact, dissimilarities between hard and soft regions of heterostructure along with the aggregation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) in interfaces could increase strength due to the formation of back stress (τb). This back stress resisted the applied stress, thereby influencing deformation. As a result, a forward stress (τf) had to overcome this back stress to allow further movement of dislocation. Back stress from dislocation interactions strengthened the material and the activation of multiple slip systems in gentler phases improved ductility. Figure  17 (e) displays the functional performance of VN phases in HEAs to activate through two various mechanisms of dislocation slip, i.e., bypassing the dislocation and cutting-through mechanisms. In bypass mechanism, dislocations were hindered by incoherent grain boundaries when they came into contact with a VN precipitate, which caused them to bend around VN phase and form dislocation loops. The extra energy needed for movement in this phase increased the resistance of the material to deformation. In cut-through mechanism, atomic misalignment resulted from dislocations that penetrated VN phase and created new surfaces. This increased surface energy and demanded more energy for dislocation motion due to dissimilar lattice parameters. This latter interaction resulted in a strengthening effect that was considerably greater than that of bypass mechanism, consequently increasing the ultimate mechanical performance. In their study, Zhang et al. [ 289 ] investigated how these mechanisms affected dislocation behaviors and the resulting rise in HEA strength.

Figure  18  summarizes some of the key strengthening and toughening mechanisms discussed in this study, as reported by various researchers. The classification presented in this figure is developed based on the literature reviewed in this study. These mechanisms include precipitation strengthening, dispersion strengthening, dislocation strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, Orowan strengthening and many other types which can be activated simultaneously for various reinforcements. The combined and interactive effects of these mechanisms play a crucial role in enhancing strength, hardness, and toughness while maintaining structural stability. Notably, the synergistic interplay between different mechanisms, such as particle strengthening and dislocation interactions, facilitates improved resistance to deformation and crack propagation. This comprehensive overview provides a clear framework for understanding the dominant factors governing mechanical behaviors and offers valuable guidance for the design and optimization of advanced HEA-based materials.

sections.heading: Conclusion, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
paragraphs: Based on the mentioned findings from various studies, oxide particles known as ODS have great effects on enhancing CYS, almost presenting the strongest effect, while showing considerable hardness and UCS. This enhancement of mechanical performance seems to be attributed to the combination of various strengthening mechanisms such as grain refinement (Zener pinning), Orowan strengthening, solid-solution strengthening and dislocation pinning, which have been frequently reported by various researchers. Borides and nitrides seem to have significant amounts of UCS and even hardness although their CYS might be smaller than oxide reinforcing agents. Their activated strengthening mechanisms can be linked to solid-solution strengthening, load transfer, grain refinement and even dislocation strengthening. Intermetallic compounds and ordered phases-such as σ phase, L1 2  precipitates, and Laves phases-also can improve hardness and UCS as a result of having ordered crystal structures and their outstanding resistance against plastic deformation. After evaluating various studies, precipitation hardening, lattice distortion, and phase-boundary strengthening were confirmed to be the most dominant mechanisms in this group. The precipitation of some coherent or semi-coherent intermetallic can prevent the movement of dislocation and make the microstructure stable, particularly at elevated temperatures; however, excessive formation of intermetallic can cause embrittlement, limiting them in load-bearing applications requiring high damage tolerance. In terms of performance, carbon-based reinforcements such as CNTs, graphene, and GNPs are used to enhance mechanical performance by helping load transfer, fracture bridging and even activation of dislocation pinning at interfaces among matrix and reinforcements. However, based on the findings of various research works, they have moderate roles in increasing ductility, hardness or strength. In fact, with respect to thermal instability and insufficient interfacial bonding during elevated-temperature processing, they show lower effectiveness compared with other groups. The obtained results have shown that the most promising group can be hybrid reinforcements, such as a combination of carbide, borides, and oxides, which can be related to the effect of combined toughening mechanisms such as Orowan, load transfer, grain refinement and precipitated particles. The findings have indicated that they are not among the highest amount of CYS and UCS, but also show considerable hardness, ultimately obtaining a great balance of ductility.

Regarding the carbides such as TiC, WC, Cr 3 C 2 , M 23 C 6 , M 7 C 3 , the findings have shown that the highest hardness and considerable UCS are mainly related to their hard nature; however, their overall ductility performance can be considered moderate or even low. Hard particles, such as TiC or SiC, resist deformation and act as effective barriers in the movement of dislocations inside HEA matrices [ 251 ]. Their significant enhancement of UCS can also be due to their intrinsic thermal stability and high hardness, consequently acting as solid load-bearing phases which can prevent dislocation movement, pinning grain boundaries and precipitation strengthening as fundamentally activated mechanisms to boost the ultimate strength. In various HEA systems, employing carbide reinforcements can specifically improve microstructure and wear resistance. Despite this, their brittleness can maximize interfacial stress, deducting the ductility and fracture toughness especially when the morphology and scattering of particles is not adequately regulated. Among various types of reinforcements, hybrid ones are mainly designed to overcome the restriction of the fabrication of single-phase microstructures by activating various strengthening mechanisms, including Orowan strengthening, load transfer, grain refining, precipitation hardening, and hybrid reinforcements. They not only exhibit considerable UCS and CYS, but also have superior ductility and fracture resistance, which make them ideal candidates for complicated structural applications which need a combination of superior strength and mechanical dependability.

The direction of future studies includes the modification of chemical composition of some specific categories. This may include novel intermetallic phases, amorphous structures, or gradient-structured composites that were not classified among the above-mentioned groups. This is one of the best ways of discovery-driven design. Other insight is that optimization can focus more on employing the mixture of various reinforcements such as carbide, oxide, boride or even various phases, typically named hybrid category. With the aim of achieving complementary reinforcement effects, future research should mainly concentrate on developing gradient and hybrid reinforcement systems that efficiently integrate several types of reinforcement such as carbonaceous nanostructures, oxides, and ceramics. In addition, given the growing importance of machine learning in materials research in recent years, along with its repeatedly-demonstrated effectiveness in the design of HEAs and their composition-mechanical property relationships, employing advanced computer modeling and machine learning is recommended to reach a better optimization of processing conditions, reinforcement types, and volume fractions [ 290 ,  291 ,  292 ,  293 ,  294 ,  295 ,  296 ,  297 ,  298 – 299 ]. In order to thoroughly comprehend various strengthening mechanisms, in-situ characterization should be performed especially during the experiments at high temperatures. The effects of various reinforcement types on the hardness of HEACs demonstrate their unique strengthening behaviors among different kinds of materials.
